rationale.text: Selected OS2 single-mode fiber with 10GBASE-ER (1550 nm) for HQ--Branch because 22000.0 m exceeds the 10 km 10GBASE-LR reach. 10GBASE-ER uses the lower-loss 1550 nm window and reaches 40 km.

rationale.standard_ref: IEEE 802.3ae channel insertion loss; TIA-568 component loss
rationale.text: Optical budget for HQ--Branch (10GBASE-ER): fiber 5.5 dB (22.0 km × 0.25 dB/km) + 2 connectors × 0.75 dB + 0 splices × 0.3 dB = 7.0 dB against 11.0 dB allowed, margin 4.0 dB (pass).

rationale.standard_ref: Project rule; physics: fiber propagation ≈ 5 µs/km
rationale.text: HQ--Branch: 22.0 km × 5.0 µs/km = 0.11 ms one-way propagation, within the 5.0 ms budget (4.89 ms left for serialization, queuing and switching). Delay-sensitive traffic still needs priority queuing so congestion does not consume that headroom.

Multi-area OSPF because the design spans 3 sites: HQ is the backbone (area 0) and every other site gets its own area, so flooding and SPF runs stay inside one site.
Area 0 (HQ) is OSPF area 0 with address block 10.20.0.0/23.
Area 1 (Branch) is OSPF area 1 with address block 10.20.2.0/24.
Area 2 (Colo) is OSPF area 2 with address block 10.20.3.0/24.
Router IDs come from Loopback0 /32 addresses. A loopback never goes down with a physical interface, so OSPF and BGP identities stay stable.

Every OSPF area uses message-digest (MD5) authentication and every adjacency interface carries the key, so a device plugged into a routed link cannot form an adjacency and inject routes. The key in the configs is a placeholder to replace before deployment.
OSPF reference bandwidth is 100000 Mbps. With the default 100 Mbps every link of 100 Mb/s or more gets cost 1, so 10G and 1G paths would look equal.
ABR BRANCH-R1 summarizes area 1 as 10.20.2.0/24 (1 route instead of 7), which works because the area's subnets were allocated from one contiguous block.
ABR COLO-R1 summarizes area 2 as 10.20.3.0/24 (1 route instead of 9), which works because the area's subnets were allocated from one contiguous block.

rationale.standard_ref: Cisco hierarchical campus design; Project rule
rationale.text: HQ: collapsed-core design (core and distribution combined) because the site has 1 building(s), below the 4-building point where a separate distribution layer pays off. Fewer devices and hops for 310 endpoints.
HQ: 310 access ports needed, so 7 × 48-port switch(es) in 1 stack(s) (≤ 8 members per stack). 26 spare port(s) are shut down.
HQ-ACC1: 60 PoE port(s) × 30.0 W (802.3at Type 2) = 1800.0 W of PoE budget required from the switch power supplies.
HQ: resiliency is high, so core switches and routers are paired and every access stack is dual-homed to both gateways. Any single device or uplink can fail without isolating users.

rationale.standard_ref: Cisco hierarchical campus design; Project rule
rationale.text: Branch: collapsed-core design (core and distribution combined) because the site has 1 building(s), below the 4-building point where a separate distribution layer pays off. Fewer devices and hops for 120 endpoints.
Branch: 120 access ports needed, so 3 × 48-port switch(es) in 1 stack(s) (≤ 8 members per stack). 24 spare port(s) are shut down.
Branch: resiliency is high, so core switches are paired and every access stack is dual-homed to both gateways. Any single device or uplink can fail without isolating users.

Colo: resiliency is high, so core switches and routers are paired and every access stack is dual-homed to both gateways. Any single device or uplink can fail without isolating users.
HQ--Branch is built as 2 circuits (HQ-R1–BRANCH-R1, HQ-R2–BRANCH-R1) so the site survives the loss of either router or circuit.
HQ--Colo is built as 2 circuits (HQ-R1–COLO-R1, HQ-R2–COLO-R2) so the site survives the loss of either router or circuit.
Native VLAN is the unused VLAN 999 on every trunk (not VLAN 1) and it is left out of the allowed lists. This blocks double-tagging VLAN hopping. Unused access ports are parked in it and shut down.
Access ports use PortFast (RSTP edge port, forwards immediately) and BPDU Guard (err-disables the port if a switch is plugged in), preventing accidental loops.
HQ: VLANs 10,20 each carry one segment, giving each role its own broadcast domain.
HQ-ACC1 trunk to HQ-CORE1 allows only VLANs 10,20, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
HQ-ACC1 trunk to HQ-CORE2 allows only VLANs 10,20, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
HQ: Rapid PVST+ root primary on HQ-CORE1 and secondary on HQ-CORE2, so the root bridge is also the default gateway and frames never take a detour through an access switch.

HQ: HSRPv2 gives each VLAN a virtual gateway (first usable address) shared by HQ-CORE1 (priority 110, active) and HQ-CORE2 (priority 100, standby). Each subnet reserves 2 extra addresses for the physical SVIs.
Branch: VLANs 110 each carry one segment, giving each role its own broadcast domain.

Colo: Rapid PVST+ root primary on COLO-CORE1 and secondary on COLO-CORE2, so the root bridge is also the default gateway and frames never take a detour through an access switch.

Branch-Users → Colo-Trading: permit tcp port 443 via ACL-BRANCH-USERS-IN, applied inbound on the Branch-Users gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
Branch-Users → Colo-Trading: deny ip via ACL-BRANCH-USERS-IN, applied inbound on the Branch-Users gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
ACL-BRANCH-USERS-IN ends with 'permit ip any any' so traffic not covered by a policy is allowed; otherwise the IOS implicit deny would drop all other traffic from Branch-Users.
